newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian communists collect food for North Korea.
newsitem.headline: Russian communists collect food for North Korea.

text.p: Russian leftists, in a Soviet-style gesture of international solidarity, said on Wednesday they plan to collect food for famine-threatened North Korea under the slogan "A kilo of rice for a Korean friend".
A spokesman for the hardline Working Russia communist group told Reuters the idea to help came from his organisation and a handful of others, including the pro-communist Officers' Union.

"There is such an initiative and several other organisations are with us," the spokesman said. He gave no details, saying what he called an "act of solidarity" with North Korean people had just started.
The move came on the day Seoul said North Korea had agreed to peace talks, in part to tackle the food shortages.
Although Russians are not starving, many are close to the poverty line. Others have become wealthy in the emerging market economy.

International aid officials say more than five million North Koreans are near starvation and could die in the next few months unless food arrives. Food is being shipped to North Korea by Christian organisations and volunteers.
North Korea was a long-time ally of the now-defunct Soviet Union but ties with Russia are less solid because Moscow has turned increasingly to other countries, including South Korea.
South Korean officials said on Wednesday Pyongyang had agreed to help arrange four-nation peace talks aimed at closing the book on the 1950-53 Korean War which split the peninsula.
Regional experts said North Korea's acceptance of the peace talks underlined how serious the food problem was. Seoul and Washington have said aid can be discussed during peace talks.
Aid officials say the food deficit in North Korea, hit by devastating floods in 1995 and 1996, is expected to be worse in 1998 than in 1997.
A growing number of North Koreans have defected to South Korea recently, many of them to avoid starvation.
Many North Koreans have come to Russia as "guest workers".

Earlier this week, Reuters Television filmed a collective farm on the outskirts of Moscow where about 100 North Koreans who grow cabbages for a pittance live in a tiny rusty wagon under portraits of their communist leaders. They still manage to send some money back home.
